title: No One Can Fix School Segregation Alone https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/school-segregation-hannah-jones-essay-education-reform.html
author: Zak Cheney-Rice
summary: Zak Cheney-Rice argues that the gleeful backlash to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay misreads what her story shows. He recounts her reasoning for choosing P.S. 307, and how the retirement of a trusted principal and disengaged teachers undid her plan. Cheney-Rice contends that Najya has the resources to recover, while most of her classmates do not, and that the uproar reveals how little society believes it should care about Black children like them. He notes that conservatives objected less to her aim than to her violating the norm that parents with means must maximize their children's advantage. Drawing on his own family's school decision in Georgia, he argues that dysfunctional schools in poor Black neighborhoods are systemic, and that unlike the coordinated desegregation movement of the 1950s and 1960s, Hannah-Jones went mostly alone. Her essay, he concludes, shows how far America is from a popular movement that might solve the problem.
points: Cheney-Rice argues that the idea Hannah-Jones ruined her daughter's future is plainly false given Najya's family resources.
A core American norm holds that parents with means are irresponsible if they fail to maximize every advantage for their children.
His own family chose a transfer lottery school because their zoned school would not answer calls to schedule a tour.
Americans have largely given up on integration and class equality as ideals, from court rulings to legislative inaction.
Unlike Jim Crow-era integrationists backed by a legal movement, Hannah-Jones acted largely alone.
quotes: One family, or even a few families, cannot transform a segregated school,” Hannah-Jones wrote at the time, “but if none of us were willing to go into them, nothing would change.

But the idea that Hannah-Jones ruined her daughter’s future in the name of foolish progressive idealism seems plainly false. Najya has all the resources she needs to recover from her deprived elementary and middle-school experiences. The same cannot be said, however, for most of her former classmates.
A core precept of the American social order is that parents with means are considered irresponsible if they fail to maximize every advantage for their children.
Our calculation was simple: Whatever extra work might be required of us to compensate for an unresponsive school was not work we felt confident we could do.
Just as poverty is systemic, so is the persistence of dysfunctional schools in poor Black neighborhoods, such that even the most active and dedicated parents will struggle to make an impact.
But the big-picture reality is that Americans have largely given up on racial integration and class equality as societal ideals.

The essay that came out of her experience is a wrenching portrait of parental guilt. But it’s also a dispiriting indication of how far we are from the kind of popular movement that might actually find a solution.
